The Power of Small Swaps

In this world, not everyone might have empathy, but I am sure they have sympathy. People might not care about rising sea levels in Tuvalu or shelter damage in Rohingya, Myanmar, but they can be sensitive enough to understand the suffering of innocent animals and children. The central challenge of climate action is not that humanity is heartless; it is that our daily systems hide environmental harm behind convenience and price tags. After a long day of class, I was heading to my dormitory in Hong Kong. The view is fantastic with a dense skyline, busy harbors with green mountain ridges. But climbing up to my dorm the temperature is too high. Since arriving here, the heat has barely relented, leaving me wondering how millions of residents endure it daily. The answer is simple. It's an air conditioning system that we use. Stepping out of the 30 degrees celsius into the freezing blast of a convenience store, it’s hard to remember that keeping this city cool swallows nearly a third of its electricity consumption making it a major indirect driver of CO2 emissions. But do people really know this fact? It’s questionable. On my way back to my dormitory, I decided to buy some meat. The wide variety of meats are available at the store shelves and I just remembered the lesson we just covered in class, 1 kg of the industrial beef needs 60kg of carbon dioxide emission to be produced. Yet I still reached for the regular industrial beef. I am not a vegetarian, and on a student budget, there was no cheaper meat option. The low CO2 alternative carried a price tag I simply could not justify. After that, I went through a Bazaar, where clothes there are so much cheaper than other stores. I checked the prices and materials. No wonder they were so cheap. It was made of Polyester, the cheapest fabric to produce. Factories make polyester from petroleum, and turning crude oil into plastic threads takes huge amounts of energy. In this way, people buy these clothes without knowing it’s cruel impact on the climate. It’s not their fault to look for cheap clothing. I also used to buy clothings made of polyester. But now I understand the better the materials, the longer it lasts. Standing outside my dorm with a bag of high-emission beef beneath the hum of air conditioners, I just realized why so many people fail to take personal responsibility. Even as someone actively studying about climate change, I fell back on habit and convenience because the impact felt abstract and the actions I am taking felt too small to matter. To move people toward genuine accountability, we cannot rely on guilt or demand overnight perfection. Instead, we need a solution rooted in visible impact and achievable small habits. Throughout my life, I observed how we perceived far better immediate feedback and social norms than than distant warnings. We talk about climate change results, but we rarely educate children and elderly about how to reduce carbon footprints. I am sure plenty of children know about global warming but are they familiar with steps they should take to reduce the impact? They better be told that there is more to do beside classifying the trash. When supermarkets display color-coded carbon footprints on food shelves, when apartments and malls show real time carbon emissions, and the clothing tags reveal the fabric emissions, the cost of consumption would become transparent. Additionally the accountability must be paired with realistic independent small actions that anyone can take financially. The steps are now easy: raising the AC by only 2 degrees, swapping the beef with chicken or vegetables once per week or choosing a cloth with good material.

When millions of individuals take small, independent ownership of their daily habits, these small actions now become significant. Not just significant but a powerful social norm. People are likely to mirror the habits of people around them, creating an effect that will attract millions more. Saving the planet doesn’t mean introducing more effective technological power plants. But very small actions that everyone can easily take in their daily lives. Hence we can’t move to Mars in decades, we need to love what we have, the Earth.

Reference; Hong Kong Electrical and Mechanical Services Department (EMSD) (Hong Kong Energy End-Use Data, Poore & Nemecek (2018) (‘Reducing food’s environmental impacts through producers and consumers’) Niinimäki et al.
